c.tagline: Habsburg-era coffee capital of western Ukraine, all cobblestones and cathedrals.

taxi.fareNote: Use ride-hailing apps (Uklon, Bolt, Uber) or a dispatch service — street taxis rarely use meters and may overcharge.

emergency.note: 112 is the general emergency number connecting to police, ambulance, and fire; 102 reaches the police and 103 the ambulance directly.

avoid.reason: No no-go districts as such, but heed air-raid alerts and keep clear of military and infrastructure sites given the ongoing war.
Pickpocketing in Rynok Square crowds and at the train station, and note the wartime curfew (roughly midnight–5am).

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed historic core around the Market Square (Ploshcha Rynok), all cobblestones, cathedrals, and centuries-old coffee houses; the best walkable base for first-time visitors.
The prosperous central district holding the fanciest hotels alongside quirky cafes, cellar bars, and reasonably priced restaurants; the hub for dining and going out.
A leafy, historic district built around the famous Lychakiv Cemetery and its parks; calm and green, ideal for history buffs and a slower pace.
A lively cultural quarter near Prospekt Svobody, close to theaters, museums, and the Opera House; an arty, buzzy feel just outside the oldest streets.
A working-class district northeast of the center below the High Castle (Vysokyi Zamok) hill; local, residential, and budget-friendly.

water.note: Tap water is not reliably potable; drink bottled or filtered.

transit.hours: Trams, trolleybuses, and marshrutka minibuses run roughly 5:30am-11pm; a few night routes cover the small hours, but taxis or ride apps fill most late-night gaps.
transit.note: Lviv has no metro; getting around relies on an extensive tram, trolleybus, and marshrutka (minibus) network, plus taxis and ride apps.
transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor in cash on board, or tap a contactless card on newer trams and trolleybuses; a single ride is about 15 UAH (~$0.37). Keep small change handy for marshrutkas.

landmarks: Rynok Square (Market Square)
The UNESCO-listed heart of Lviv rings its Renaissance town hall with 44 pastel merchant houses, four corner fountains, and the city's liveliest café terraces.
Lviv Opera House
This opulent 1900 Viennese-style theater, crowned by winged bronze muses, anchors Svobody Avenue and offers world-class performances for remarkably modest prices.
High Castle Hill (Vysokyi Zamok)
The wooded mound of Lviv's vanished fortress rewards climbers with a 360-degree panorama over a sea of domes, spires, and red-tiled roofs.
Lychakiv Cemetery
One of Europe's great necropolises, this romantic hillside labyrinth of sculpted angels and ivy-clad tombs shelters Ukrainian and Polish luminaries beneath ancient trees.
Latin Cathedral (Cathedral Basilica of the Assumption)
Lviv's Gothic-baroque Roman Catholic cathedral, consecrated in 1481, glows with jewel-toned stained glass and centuries of Polish royal history.
Armenian Cathedral
Hidden in a cobbled courtyard, this 1363 cathedral entrances with haunting early-20th-century frescoes and mosaics blending Armenian tradition with Secession style.
Boim Chapel
The blackened stone facade of this 1615 family mausoleum is carved floor-to-finial with biblical scenes, a Mannerist tour de force beside the Latin Cathedral.
Dominican Church (Church of the Holy Eucharist)
A monumental green dome crowns this baroque masterpiece modeled on Vienna's Karlskirche, its curved facade commanding one of the old town's finest squares.
St. George's Cathedral
The mother church of Ukrainian Greek Catholicism crowns St. George's Hill in yellow rococo splendor, its terrace overlooking the city it long shepherded.
Potocki Palace
This mirror-halled French-style palace of the Potocki counts now displays European old-master paintings as a grand branch of the Lviv National Art Gallery.

intl.to: Prague & Kraków (Czechia/Poland) - through booking with a change at Przemyśl

train.note: International and domestic trains use Lviv-Holovnyi, the 1904 art nouveau station about 2 km west of the centre and reached by tram 1 or 9. With Ukrainian airspace closed to civil aviation, rail is the main way into the country: the cross-border trains run to Przemyśl Główny in Poland, where Ukrainian broad gauge meets standard gauge, and passport and customs checks there or at Mostyska can add an hour or two to the journey. Book on booking.uz.gov.ua as far ahead as the sales window allows, since cross-border seats disappear quickly, and expect timetables to shift with air-raid alerts. Overnight trains also link Lviv with Kyiv, Odesa and Kharkiv, and services run east to Chop for onward connections into Hungary and Slovakia.

intl.to: Warsaw, Kraków, Katowice, Lublin & Rzeszów (Poland), Berlin, Munich & Hamburg (Germany), Prague & Brno (Czechia), Budapest (Hungary)

bus.note: FlixBus uses two stops in Lviv, outside the main railway station and at the Stryiskyi bus station, and lists around 95 directly reachable cities. Most other international coaches leave from Bus Station No. 1 on Stryiska Street, about 6 km south of the centre, with services to Warsaw, Przemyśl, Lublin, Wrocław and Prague; stations No. 2 and No. 8 handle regional and domestic routes. Buses often work out quicker than the train into Poland because there is no gauge change, but the road crossings at Krakovets, Shehyni and Rava-Ruska can involve long queues, so allow several hours at the frontier. Buy online in advance where possible; counter sales are cash in hryvnia.

ferry.note: Lviv is an inland city in western Ukraine, roughly 600 km from the Black Sea and on no navigable river, so no passenger boat services exist.

half.name: Olesko Castle
half.blurb: A 14th-century castle on a hill about 65 kilometers from Lviv, birthplace of Polish king Jan III Sobieski, now a museum of art.

half.name: Pidhirtsi Castle
half.blurb: A 17th-century palace-fortress near Lviv built in Italian Renaissance style, part of the same Golden Horseshoe castle route as Olesko.

half.name: Zolochiv Castle
half.blurb: A restored 17th-century fortress east of Lviv with a Chinese-style pavilion in its courtyard, the third stop on the Golden Horseshoe route.

full.name: Truskavets
full.blurb: A spa town in the Carpathian foothills known for mineral springs, particularly the sulfurous Naftusia water used in local treatment sanatoriums.
